title: Pinocchio is hungry and finds an egg to make an omelette; but just at the best moment, the omelette flies out of the window.
paragraphs: Meanwhile it began to grow dark, and Pinocchio, remembering that he had eaten nothing, felt a little ache in his stomach that was very much like an appetite.
But a child’s appetite moves fast, and sure enough, after a few minutes his appetite became hunger, and in the blink of an eye that hunger became a wolf’s hunger, a hunger you could cut with a knife.

Poor Pinocchio ran straight to the fireplace, where a pot was boiling, and reached to lift the lid and see what was inside: but the pot was painted on the wall. Imagine how he felt. His nose, which was already long, grew at least another four fingers’ width.

Then he began running around the room and searching every little box and cupboard for a bit of bread, even dry bread, a little crust, a bone the dog had left, some mouldy corn porridge, a fishbone, a cherry stone, in short anything to chew: but he found nothing, absolutely nothing, nothing at all.

And meanwhile his hunger grew and kept on growing: and poor Pinocchio had no comfort except yawning, and his yawns were so long that sometimes his mouth stretched as far as his ears. And after yawning he spat, and felt his stomach fading away.
Then, crying in despair, he said:
“The Talking Cricket was right. I was wrong to turn against my dad and run away from home… If my dad were here now, I wouldn’t be dying of yawns! Oh! What a terrible illness hunger is!”
Just then he thought he saw something round and white in the rubbish heap that looked exactly like a hen’s egg. In a single instant he leapt and pounced on it. It really was an egg.

It is impossible to describe the puppet’s joy: you must imagine it for yourself. Hardly believing it was not a dream, he turned the egg over in his hands, and touched it and kissed it, and as he kissed it he said:

“And now how shall I cook it? Shall I make an omelette?… No, better to cook it in a dish!… Or wouldn’t it taste better if I fried it in a pan? Or what if I soft-boiled it so I could drink it? No, the quickest way of all is to cook it in a dish or a little pan: I’m too eager to eat it!”

No sooner said than done, he put a little pan over a pot full of glowing coals: he put a little water into the pan instead of oil or butter: and when the water began to steam, crack!… he broke the eggshell and went to tip the egg into it.
But instead of the white and yolk, out popped a cheerful, very polite chick, which made a fine bow and said:
“A thousand thanks, Mr Pinocchio, for saving me the trouble of breaking the shell! Goodbye, keep well, and give everyone at home my best wishes!”
Having said this, it spread its wings, shot through the open window, and flew away out of sight.

The poor puppet stayed there as if under a spell, with staring eyes, an open mouth, and the eggshells in his hands. But when he recovered from his first shock, he began to cry, scream, and stamp his feet in despair, and as he cried he said:
“And the Talking Cricket was right after all! If I hadn’t run away from home and my dad were here, I wouldn’t be dying of hunger now. Oh! What a terrible illness hunger is!…”

And because his stomach kept growling worse than ever, and he did not know how to quiet it, he decided to leave the house and run to the nearby village, hoping to find some kind person who would give him a little bread.
